lines.text: A country of rainforest on the Atlantic shore, rich in oil and wildlife, ruled for half a century by one family. This is the story of Gabon.
In 1849 the French settled freed slaves on the coast at a place they called Libreville, the free town. It is now the capital.
In 1913 the doctor and thinker Albert Schweitzer opened a hospital at Lambarene, deep in the forest. His work there earned him the Nobel Peace Prize.
Leon Mba, born in 1902, would lead the country to independence and become its first president.
Omar Bongo, born in 1935, would follow him in 1967 and rule until his death in 2009, one of the longest reigns of any leader in the world.
In 1946 the Lope reserve was set aside, a mosaic of forest and savanna that is now a World Heritage Site.
In 1959 Ali Bongo was born, the son who would inherit his father's presidency.
In 1960 Gabon became independent from France. Oil would soon make it one of the richest countries in Africa.
Brice Oligui Nguema, born in 1975, would rise to command the presidential guard, and then turn on the family it guarded.
In 1989 Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang was born, the striker who would become Gabon's leading goalscorer.
In 2002 Loango National Park was created, where elephants and hippos wander down onto the beaches.
In 2012 Gabon co-hosted the Africa Cup of Nations, and football filled its streets.
And in August 2023 the army seized power, ending fifty-six years of Bongo rule. Two years later its leader was elected president.
Its forests still stand, and Gabon now turns a new page after the Bongo years.
